chapter_theme: Dreams as the woman's way of staying alive. She argues that a lover who won't come when she is awake comes when she sleeps, and so waking life is the villain and the gossips are simply people who have never dreamed of a beloved.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's in Parimelazhagar's reading, except that Manakkudavar gives 1211 to the friend. Parimelazhagar sees her first praising the dream and using it to reassure her friend (1211-1216), then pained on waking (1217), and finally defending the man against the friend's blame (1218-1220).

1211.reading: What feast can be given to the dream that came with a message from the lover? The speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
1211.nuance: The Kural's great social duty of hospitality is turned on a dream guest. Parimelazhagar's little note gets the joke exactly: it is a guest for which one can find nothing to serve.

positions.position: The woman herself saw the dream and says this.
The friend says she dreamed that messengers came, in order to comfort the woman.
positions.quote: இது தலைமகளாற்றுதற் பொருட்டுக் காதலர் வாராநின்றாரென்று தூதர் வாக் கனாக் கண்டேனென்று தோழி சொல்லியது.

1212.reading: The woman says that if her carp-like kohl-lined eyes would sleep when she begs them to, she would tell the one who joined with her that she is surviving.
1212.nuance: She must beg her eyes for sleep, after cursing them in chapter 118. Parimelazhagar notes her reason for preferring this to a messenger: there are things kept back from messengers, or shortened, which she could tell him in full.

1213.reading: The woman says her life continues because she sees in her dreams the man who gives no grace in waking life.
1213.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes it as a reassurance to the friend who worries: 'don't worry, I'm bearing up'. It may comfort the friend, but what it actually says is hardly comforting.

1214.reading: The woman says there is pleasure in dreams, since they seek out and bring her the man who gives no grace in waking life.
1214.nuance: The dream becomes an agent, a go-between travelling to where he is. That is what she wanted from her friend. Manakkudavar has the friend ask what use a dream is without real enjoyment, and the verse is her answer.

1215.reading: The woman says that what she saw in waking life was sweet only then, and likewise the dream is sweet at the time it is seen.
1215.nuance: A strong philosophical move: both are equally over when over. Waking joy has no special standing in memory. Parimelazhagar's gloss is plain: 'the two are equal for me', and what she had before was no more than this.

1216.reading: The woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover in the dream wouldn't leave.
1216.nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies a charged word, பாவி, 'sinner', for waking, and reads ஒன்று as pointing up its cruelty. Waking is what barges in and parts them, so the person responsible for leaving is no longer him but waking itself.

1217.reading: The woman asks why the cruel one who gives no grace in waking life torments her in dreams.
1217.nuance: A flat reversal of the last six verses, with the comfort now a torment. Parimelazhagar explains: on waking she doesn't find him, and because he vanishes from her shoulder, that too brings pain. He also tests a proverb against her case, that what isn't in waking isn't in dreams.

1218.reading: The woman says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
1218.nuance: In Parimelazhagar's reading she is defending him against her friend: he never leaves her at all. விரைந்து, 'quickly', gives the speed of a fugitive, and Manakkudavar hears the friend's tease that prompted it: where does he go when sleep ends?

1219.reading: The woman says those who haven't seen their lovers in dreams are the ones who blame the man for not being gracious in waking life.
1219.nuance: This is an attack by pretending to speak about outsiders, as both commentators note. For Parimelazhagar she is hinting that the friend has no lover, which is a harsh thing to imply, and marks how angry the blaming makes her.

1220.reading: The woman says that the people of this town say he has left her in waking life, and asks if they don't see him in dreams.
1220.nuance: A surreal question, since no one else could see her dream. Parimelazhagar makes sense of it by way of the unity between her and her friend: if they are truly one, what the woman saw, the friend has seen too, and in not seeing she has become an outsider, 'this town'.

links.note: 81 says the whole point of keeping a home is to tend guests. 1211 applies that duty to a dream, which can be neither fed nor refused. A woman with an empty house is still measuring her situation in terms of the householder's virtue.

In Parimelazhagar's reading of 1162, sending a message shames her because it implies she's still alive. In 1212, telling him she has survived is just what she wants, provided it's in a dream. The dream permits what her waking shame forbids.

339 says death is like sleep and birth is like waking from it, as an image of impermanence. 1216 wishes waking away altogether, for the sake of staying with her lover. If the two were read together, her wish would come close to a wish not to be reborn, though nothing in the verse says this.
Both end by accusing this town of not understanding. In 1130 he dwells in her heart, while in 1220 he comes in her dreams. The defence moves on as her grounds grow thinner.

source_issues: 1216: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is essentially the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss, including the word பாவி, so it isn't independent.
1212: Manakkudavar's entry has கடலுண்கண் where the verse has கயலுண்கண், apparently a typo.
